title: Field Kit: Templates for the Marketplace Architect
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published index.md (unit for unit, in its own order) and spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces. Intent outcome, the three acceptance criteria and the role are copied unchanged from the toolkit's entry in journal-spec.json; the journal entry has no thesis object, so the thesis below is written here from the entry's question, the Reference part's supporting claim R-1 and the published page. The introduction realises the Reference part's opening (hook, bridge, roadmap). Tables and fenced template blocks are not units; each is recorded as the evidence of the unit before it.

know: The twelve templates (capability map row and heat map, vertical requirement profile, listing lifecycle state table, attribute dictionary entry, feed contract, publication-pipeline SLA card, search index design card, trust-and-safety policy-to-enforcement card, entitlement matrix, listing event specification, consolidation decision card, architecture decision record), the chapter behind each, and the three conventions they share (maintained data, references by identifier, a Veldmark example).
can_do: Find the template for a design or decision from the question it answers, copy it and fill only the fields that change the decision, writing 'unknown' rather than guessing.
Say which fields carry ownership, removal behavior and dates, and avoid the three common mistakes listed for each template.

audience.who: Chief and enterprise architects of marketplace groups, principal engineers, search, data, trust-and-safety and monetization leads and platform-engineering leads who need a working form for a decision; product and commercial leaders use Tools 1, 2, 9 and 11 as discussion documents.
already_knows: What an API, a database, an event stream, a search engine and Kubernetes are.
The book's chapters, or how to open the owning chapter linked from each tool.
Veldmark and its brands (Tradeyard, Motorvane, Hearthly, Keybridge), as introduced in meet-veldmark, and the failure-pattern names of where-listing-systems-go-wrong.
does_not_know: Which of the book's records fits the decision on their desk.
Which fields of each record are dropped first.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given three decisions, the reader finds the template for each from the page's lookup table and names the owning chapter and one field that must not be dropped.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: which template do you use to (a) agree a bulk feed with a new dealer-software vendor, (b) decide whether to move an acquired brand's search onto the group platform, and (c) define what a paid package does to a listing and how it is billed? For each, name the chapter behind it and one field you must not leave out.
acceptance_criteria.expected: (a) Tool 5, the feed contract (listing-ingestion), with what absence means, field ownership, removal latency or the mass-change guard; (b) Tool 11, the consolidation decision card (platform-consolidation, with the advice process of organizing-marketplace-engineering), with the gate or rollback and the cost to reverse, or Tool 12's decision record; (c) Tool 9, the entitlement matrix (products-and-entitlements), with its effects, enforcement points, failure behavior or billing basis.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can say what the page contains, how to use it and which fields matter most.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this page give you, how should you use it, and which fields does it say get dropped first?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Twelve working templates for the records Parts I to VIII ask a Chief Architect to keep, each with a Veldmark example, common mistakes and the owning chapter; start with the record that changes the decision this week, keep the templates as maintained data cited by identifier; the fields for ownership, removal behavior and dates are dropped first.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the page, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: Which template turns the decision on the reader's desk into a working record, and which of its fields must not be dropped?
thesis.claim: A decision's template is found from the question it answers, filled only where the decision changes and kept as maintained data cited by identifier, and the fields that must not be dropped are those for ownership, removal behavior and dates: seven of the twelve templates record what happens when a listing ends, and the incidents the Veldmark examples replay (38,400 cars unpublished by truncated files, a sold bike in 214 digests, a fraud rule nobody was assigned to carry to Motorvane) each came from one of those fields left blank.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that templates are sample forms to fill in completely, or to copy once into a slide deck, with every field equally worth keeping.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect copies the one template for this week's decision, keeps it where the system it describes lives, writes 'unknown' rather than guessing, and fills the owner, removal and date fields before any other.
thesis.how_why: Each tool gives a purpose, when to use it, the fields to copy, one Veldmark example and three common mistakes, and links its owning chapter; the examples replay the book's incidents and show the field that now prevents each, and the records cite each other by identifier (`POL-FRAUD-PAYLINK` v3, `listing.events.v1`, `pro-150@v5`) so a stale listing can be followed back to the contract that allowed it.

supporting_claims.claim: A reader finds the template from the question on their desk, through a lookup table that names one tool and its owning chapter per question, and a diagram shows how the records point to each other.

Each template is the smallest form that makes one recurring decision explicit and gives it an owner: a purpose, when to use it, fields to copy, one Veldmark example and three common mistakes, with the owning chapter for the reasoning; a reader fills only the fields that change the decision and writes 'unknown' rather than guessing.

The fields that must not be dropped carry ownership, removal behavior and dates: seven of the twelve templates record what happens when a listing ends, and each incident the Veldmark examples replay came from one of those fields left blank and is now prevented by it.
The templates stay true only as maintained data that cite each other by identifier, kept in a register where records are superseded rather than edited.

role.contribution: Turns the book's recurring decisions into twelve copyable records and performs the reference part's opening.

additional_patterns.applies_to: tool-1 to tool-12: the order of the parts that teach them (understand, model, supply, discover, trust, money, platform, lead), with the decision record last because every other tool feeds it

flow.rationale: A reader arrives with one decision, so the page first gives the whole set as a lookup (the table) and as a chain (the diagram), then each template, then how to keep them true. The tools follow the order of the parts that teach them, so a reader can move between a tool and its chapter in reading order, and citations run mostly backward (the index card cites the dictionary's purposes, the decision record every other tool). A few point forward (the SLA card and the index card rest on the consumer registry, the event contract and the effect projector of Tools 9 and 10); the lookup table and the tool anchors make those reachable, and part order is kept because moving Tool 10 earlier would separate it from the platform chapters that teach it. Put the tools before the lookup and the reader would have to read twelve templates to find one; put the decision record anywhere but last and its citations would point forward to most of the records it cites.

hook.content: These are working templates for a group of listing marketplaces: the records that Parts I to VIII ask a Chief Architect to keep.

bridge.from_reader_world: The decisions argued in Parts I to VIII, from the capability map to the decision record, which a reader has met as chapters.
bridge.to_topic: The records a team keeps for those decisions, each tested against Veldmark and kept as maintained data, not documents.

thesis_statement.text: Find the record that changes the decision on your desk, fill only the fields that change it, and keep the fields that carry ownership, removal behavior and dates: they are dropped first, seven of the twelve templates record what happens when a listing ends, and the records cite each other by identifier.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout (all three bullets) and paragraph p01's last two sentences.

roadmap.placement: Paragraph p03, after the three conventions.

promises.promise: A table that finds the template for the question on the reader's desk.
A diagram of how the records cite each other.
The twelve tools in the order of the parts that teach them, each with purpose, when to use it, template, Veldmark example, common mistakes and owning chapter.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: These are working templates for a group of listing marketplaces, the records Parts I to VIII ask a Chief Architect to keep, and the reader should adapt their wording but keep the fields for ownership, removal behavior and dates, which are dropped first and whose absence the next incident finds.

evidence.what: From the capability map of business-capabilities to the decision record of organizing-marketplace-engineering, each tested against Veldmark; not a certification scheme or a vendor method; the smallest form that makes a decision explicit, assigns an owner and leaves evidence someone else can check.
evidence.shows: Places the page in the book and names the fields that matter most, so the reader knows what to protect when trimming a template.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three conventions run through all twelve templates: they are maintained data rather than documents, they reference each other by identifier, and each has a short Veldmark example consistent with the chapter that teaches it.

evidence.what: Where each record lives (architecture repository, taxonomy and attribute service, beside the registered schema, policy registry, catalog, one Git register); a template copied into a slide deck stops being true within a quarter; examples of records citing each other; all Veldmark names, figures and dates fictional and illustrative.
evidence.shows: Tells the reader how to keep and connect the records before meeting any of them.

transition_in.carries_over: The records the page offers and the fields to keep.
transition_in.introduces: The three conventions every record follows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The page starts with a table that finds the template for the question on the reader's desk and a diagram of how the records cite each other, then gives the twelve tools in the order of the parts that teach them, each with its purpose, when to use it, the template, a Veldmark example, three common mistakes and its owning chapter, and ends with how to keep the templates true over time and where the glossary and bibliography take over.

evidence.what: The page's sections in order and the two reference pages that follow it.
evidence.shows: Lets a reader of the opening predict the page and use it as a lookup.

transition_in.introduces: The map of the page that holds them.

sections.heading: Find the Template for the Question on Your Desk
sections.controlling_idea: A reader finds the template for a decision from the question it answers, not by reading the twelve in order.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the lookup that turns a question into one template and its chapter.

transition_in.introduces: The lookup table.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Start from the question in the middle column of the lookup table; each row names one tool, links to it and names the chapter that owns it.

evidence.what: Twelve rows: Tool | Use it when | Chapter, from the capability map (business-capabilities) to the architecture decision record (organizing-marketplace-engineering).
evidence.shows: A reader with a decision can find its template and owning chapter in one look.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three records owned by other chapters (the tenant register and configuration hierarchy, the qualified-contact definition and the journey SLOs) are linked from the tools that depend on them, not repeated here.

transition_in.carries_over: The twelve templates the table lists.
transition_in.introduces: The records it deliberately leaves to other chapters.

sections.heading: How the Records Connect
sections.controlling_idea: Most changes in a marketplace group pass through several tools, and each record points to the next by identifier.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that the records form one chain a reader can follow, which is why they cite each other by identifier.

transition_in.carries_over: The tools listed one per row.
transition_in.introduces: How the same tools refer to each other.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Most changes in a marketplace group pass through several of the tools in one direction: understanding records feed decisions, decisions produce the listing's model and its contracts, and the operational records rest on the event specification and the SLA card.

evidence.what: Figure 1: understanding records feed decisions; decisions produce the listing's model and its contracts; nearly every operational record rests on the event specification and the SLA card.
evidence.shows: The caption says why: a change is finished only when every copy of the listing reflects it, so the records that carry changes to every copy sit underneath the rest.

sections.heading: Tool 1: Capability Map Row and Heat Map
sections.controlling_idea: The capability map row and heat map score each capability's differentiation, maturity and duplication so that sharing, investment and ownership are argued from the same evidence.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the frame every later record cites.

flow.rationale: Every tool uses the same order so a reader who has used one can scan the next: what the record is, then when to reach for it, then the fields to copy, then the fields filled once for Veldmark, then the mistakes that make it useless, then the chapter that holds the reasoning. The mistakes name fields, so they need the template before them; the example fills the template, so it cannot come first.

transition_in.carries_over: The diagram, whose understanding records feed every decision.
transition_in.introduces: The first of them, the capability map.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A capability map describes what the marketplace must be able to do independent of system, team or brand, and its heat map scores each level-2 capability on differentiation, maturity and duplication, so it is the stable frame every later record cites.
Use the map for sharing decisions, consolidation cases, portfolio discussions and any capability with no named owner, and refresh it before annual planning and after every acquisition.

transition_in.introduces: The occasions that call for it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The template is one row per level-2 capability, with level 3 only where a decision needs it.

evidence.what: Twelve fields from ID and level-1 area to Reading, including Owner, Maturity per implementation with dated evidence, Duplication verdict and Linked decision.
evidence.shows: Shows which fields carry the owner, the dated evidence and the decision that chose the verdict.

transition_in.introduces: The record itself, field by field, to copy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark's map v1 of 31 March 2027 fills the row for 3.1 Search and filtering.

evidence.what: Three engines; maturity Tradeyard 2, Motorvane 4, Hearthly 3; verdict split at level 3; annual run cost about €11.8M; linked to the 14 September 2027 search decision.
evidence.shows: Shows a filled row whose verdict follows from its scores.

transition_in.introduces: The same template filled in once for Veldmark.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The verdict follows from the scores: the engine differentiates little and is run three times, while relevance differentiates each brand, so the machinery is shared and the ranking is not.

transition_in.introduces: Why its verdict follows from its scores.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three mistakes make the map useless: one maturity score per capability, one group scoring everything, and forgetting the deliberate duplicate.

evidence.what: Keybridge's listing distribution and Hearthly's feed ingestion duplicated on purpose under the March 2027 neutrality decision.
evidence.shows: A map without a 'keep separate' verdict invites a cost program to merge what was kept apart on purpose.

transition_in.carries_over: The filled row and its verdict.
transition_in.introduces: The three ways the record most often goes wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The owning chapter is business-capabilities.

transition_in.carries_over: The template, its example and its mistakes.
transition_in.introduces: The owning chapter, which works the full reasoning.

sections.heading: Tool 2: Vertical Requirement Profile and Share-Layer Row
sections.controlling_idea: The vertical requirement profile describes a vertical by the forces acting on its systems, and its share-layer row records which layer each part of a capability sits in and the gate a vertical must pass to move onto it.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the evidence a sharing decision needs per vertical.

flow.rationale: Every tool uses the same order so a reader who has used one can scan the next: what the record is, then when to reach for it, then the fields to copy, then the fields filled once for Veldmark, then the mistakes that make it useless, then the chapter that holds the reasoning. The mistakes name fields, so they need the template before them; the example fills the template, so it cannot come first.

transition_in.carries_over: The capability rows, scored across the group.
transition_in.introduces: One vertical's forces, which decide where a shared capability may serve it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A vertical requirement profile describes a vertical by fourteen dimensions of the forces on its systems, and the share-layer row records which of four layers each part of a capability sits in and on what condition a vertical moves onto it.

Use the profile when a vertical is asked to move onto a shared engine, a new vertical or country section is proposed, or a vertical's business model changes; it goes into the decision record as evidence.

transition_in.introduces: The occasions that call for it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The template is one page per vertical, numbers first, with the share-layer row beside it.

evidence.what: Fourteen dimensions in five groups (Supply, Item, Demand, Money, Rules) and the share-layer row block with layer, owner, reason, stage gate, extension points and review trigger.
evidence.shows: Shows the profile records forces as numbers and the row records an owner and a gate.

transition_in.introduces: The record itself, field by field, to copy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark's Motorvane DE profile, ratified April 2027, fills the dimensions with numbers.

evidence.what: 91% of listings from 21,400 dealers; 88% of dealer listings by DMS feed; the Golf sold in 15 days with the feed delete 26 hours later; Pro 150 at €1,450 a month.
evidence.shows: Shows forces stated as numbers that decide removal and monetization design.

transition_in.introduces: The same template filled in once for Veldmark.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The share-layer row places vehicle identity, specification and price rating at layer 3, owned by Motorvane and consumed by Tradeyard Poland's cars section, and gates Motorvane's move onto the shared ingestion engine on feed success rate and delete latency.

evidence.what: Tradeyard Poland's cars section: about 410,000 live listings, about 40% from dealers; stage gate: feed success rate and delete latency no worse than Motorvane reports today.
evidence.shows: Shows a layer, an owner, a consumer and a gate in one row.

transition_in.introduces: The share-layer row built from it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three mistakes make the profile useless: profiling features instead of forces, classifying a whole capability into one layer, and omitting the stage gate.

transition_in.carries_over: The profile and its share-layer row.
transition_in.introduces: The three ways the record most often goes wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The owning chapter is vertical-requirements.

transition_in.carries_over: The template, its example and its mistakes.
transition_in.introduces: The owning chapter, which works the full reasoning.

sections.heading: Tool 3: Listing Lifecycle State Table
sections.controlling_idea: The listing lifecycle state table makes every state, transition, trigger and derived behavior explicit, separating the listing's publication state from trust and safety's enforcement overlay.

advances_thesis.how: Its derived-behavior and outcome fields carry what happens when a listing ends.

flow.rationale: Every tool uses the same order so a reader who has used one can scan the next: what the record is, then when to reach for it, then the fields to copy, then the fields filled once for Veldmark, then the mistakes that make it useless, then the chapter that holds the reasoning. The mistakes name fields, so they need the template before them; the example fills the template, so it cannot come first.

transition_in.carries_over: The understanding records of Part I.
transition_in.introduces: The listing's own model, from Part II, starting with its states.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A listing lifecycle is the set of states, transitions, triggers and per-state behavior, and the state table separates the publication state owned by the listing from the enforcement overlay owned by trust and safety, deriving visibility from both.
Use the table when designing a listing service, adding a state, integrating a vertical with other words, or investigating why a listing is live in one system and gone in another.

transition_in.introduces: The occasions that call for it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The template is two tables and a list.

transition_in.introduces: The record itself, field by field, to copy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The first table records transitions: from, to, trigger, command, event emitted and whether an outcome code is required.

evidence.what: Transitions table with an outcome code required for every terminal transition.
evidence.shows: Shows every end of a listing must record an outcome.

transition_in.carries_over: The three parts of the template.
transition_in.introduces: The first: transitions.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The second table records the behavior derived for each publication state and overlay.

evidence.what: Derived behavior per state: searchable, detail page, contactable, alertable and recommendable, URL behavior (200 / 404 / 410), retention clock.
evidence.shows: Shows visibility is derived per state, not stored in many places.

transition_in.introduces: The second table: behavior per state.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The list records the rules: who may set which states, the three timestamps, the outcome vocabulary for terminal transitions, and the vertical mappings.

transition_in.introduces: The rules to record beside them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark's Common Ground lifecycle for Tradeyard goods fills the derived-behavior table.

evidence.what: Active, restricted, held or blocked, Reserved, Sold, Withdrawn and Archived, with searchable, contactable, alertable and URL behavior for each.
evidence.shows: Shows Sold as not alertable, the rule the bike's digest broke.

transition_in.introduces: The same template filled in once for Veldmark.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Rotterdam bike exercises the table: reserved at 14:02 and sold at 18:10 on 8 March 2027 with outcome sold on platform for €225, removed from search at 18:11, and still in a digest assembled at 17:30 that broke the table's 'Alertable: No' for Sold.

evidence.what: Active at 19:48 on Sunday 7 March 2027; `ListingReserved` at 14:02 on Monday 8 March; `ListingSold` at 18:10; €225 in the outcome, not the price; Hearthly and Motorvane vertical mappings.
evidence.shows: Shows the outcome field and the alertable rule at work on one listing.

transition_in.introduces: One listing walked through it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three mistakes make the table useless: one status column for three owners, treating a bump or renewal as a new listing, and ending listings without an outcome.

transition_in.carries_over: The bike walked through the table.
transition_in.introduces: The three ways the record most often goes wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The owning chapter is listing-aggregate.

transition_in.carries_over: The template, its example and its mistakes.
transition_in.introduces: The owning chapter, which works the full reasoning.

sections.heading: Tool 4: Attribute Dictionary Entry
sections.controlling_idea: The attribute dictionary entry is a small contract for one attribute that keeps facets, filters, feeds and trust rules agreeing about what a listing is.

advances_thesis.how: Records the owner, purposes and dated requiredness of each attribute.

flow.rationale: Every tool uses the same order so a reader who has used one can scan the next: what the record is, then when to reach for it, then the fields to copy, then the fields filled once for Veldmark, then the mistakes that make it useless, then the chapter that holds the reasoning. The mistakes name fields, so they need the template before them; the example fills the template, so it cannot come first.

transition_in.carries_over: The lifecycle table, which models the listing's states.
transition_in.introduces: The dictionary, which models the listing's attributes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An attribute dictionary entry is a small contract for one attribute (key, meaning, type, unit, values, scope, purposes, provenance precedence, owner) that the schema compiler turns into forms, validators, index mappings and feed mappings.
Use an entry when an attribute is proposed, about to become required, has its value list changed, or turns out to share a meaning with another key or carry two meanings.

transition_in.introduces: The occasions that call for it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The template builds on the public models of eBay's Taxonomy API and Amazon's product type definitions.

evidence.what: Fifteen fields from Key to Owner and status, including Requiredness by category with an expected-required date and Purposes.
evidence.shows: Shows the dates and owner an entry must carry and the purposes that drive what it compiles into.

transition_in.introduces: The record itself, field by field, to copy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark's `bike.battery_capacity_wh` entry, from schema release 2027.11, fills the template.

evidence.what: Recommended from 1 November 2027, required on create and revise from 1 March 2028, a four-month runway for dealer feeds; seller, then partner_feed, then model precedence.
evidence.shows: Shows a dated requiredness runway and a precedence rule in one entry.

transition_in.introduces: The same template filled in once for Veldmark.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The rollout followed the producer-breaking rule: publish the field and a readiness report per feed, validate with warnings during the runway, and only then return a stable error code.

transition_in.introduces: How the rollout used it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three mistakes make an entry useless: changing meaning, unit or type in place, converting what cannot be converted, and leaving purposes blank.

evidence.what: Tradeyard's cleanup found 31 of 990 retired keys still read by something.
evidence.shows: Shows that blank purposes hide an attribute's readers.

transition_in.introduces: The three ways the record most often goes wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The owning chapter is attribute-schemas.

transition_in.carries_over: The template, its example and its mistakes.
transition_in.introduces: The owning chapter, which works the full reasoning.

sections.heading: Tool 5: Feed Contract
sections.controlling_idea: The feed contract is everything both sides must agree on for a supply channel to be operable, of which schema validity is perhaps a third.

advances_thesis.how: Its semantics and reconciliation clauses state what absence means and hold a truncated file.

flow.rationale: Every tool uses the same order so a reader who has used one can scan the next: what the record is, then when to reach for it, then the fields to copy, then the fields filled once for Veldmark, then the mistakes that make it useless, then the chapter that holds the reasoning. The mistakes name fields, so they need the template before them; the example fills the template, so it cannot come first.

transition_in.carries_over: The listing's model from Part II.
transition_in.introduces: Supply from Part III, which writes into that model.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A feed contract covers scope, identity, semantics, field ownership, schema, timeliness, media, errors, limits, reconciliation and change management, and it is a product artifact because partners judge a marketplace by how predictable its feed is.
Every channel that writes listings gets one, including the insertion flow, and especially any channel whose removal behavior is unknown.

transition_in.introduces: The occasions that call for it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The template is a contract block to copy.

evidence.what: A YAML block from feed_contract to change_management, with absence_means, field_ownership, status-change timeliness and a mass-change guard.
evidence.shows: Shows removal semantics, ownership and the guard as named clauses.

transition_in.introduces: The record itself, field by field, to copy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark's Motorvane DMS channel under Supply Contract v1 fills the contract.

evidence.what: Hybrid mode: daily snapshot at 17:00 and status deltas within 15 minutes; content hash with about 91% unchanged; one RFC 9457 error catalog; mass-change guard on the snapshot.
evidence.shows: Shows each clause filled with a number or a rule.

transition_in.introduces: The same template filled in once for Veldmark.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The contract replaces two incidents with two controls: the truncated files that unpublished 38,400 cars for 286 dealers become 286 held runs, and the Golf's 26-hour-late removal becomes a 15-minute status delta.

evidence.what: Truncated files of Monday 8 March 2027, 38,400 cars for 286 dealers by 02:55; the Golf removed 26 hours late.
evidence.shows: Ties each control in the contract to the incident it prevents.

transition_in.introduces: The incidents its clauses prevent.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three mistakes make a contract useless: leaving 'absence means removal' implicit, purging the external-key mapping on removal, and giving one partner a private door.

transition_in.carries_over: The contract and the incidents it prevents.
transition_in.introduces: The three ways the record most often goes wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The owning chapter is listing-ingestion.

transition_in.carries_over: The template, its example and its mistakes.
transition_in.introduces: The owning chapter, which works the full reasoning.

sections.heading: Tool 6: Publication-Pipeline SLA Card
sections.controlling_idea: The SLA card turns 'listings should go live fast' into a contract of coverage, clock and removal with a budget per stage, and treats removal as a separate, stricter promise.

advances_thesis.how: Its removal row names an objective for every registered consumer.

flow.rationale: Every tool uses the same order so a reader who has used one can scan the next: what the record is, then when to reach for it, then the fields to copy, then the fields filled once for Veldmark, then the mistakes that make it useless, then the chapter that holds the reasoning. The mistakes name fields, so they need the template before them; the example fills the template, so it cannot come first.

transition_in.carries_over: Records arriving through a feed contract.
transition_in.introduces: The pipeline that makes them searchable, and later removes them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The SLA card states a time-to-searchable target with coverage, clock and removal and a per-stage budget that adds up to it, so the fast path cannot be met by holding more listings, and removal is a stricter promise of its own.
Use the card when setting a time-to-searchable target, accepting a new channel or vertical, adding a stage, or registering a new consumer of listing data.

transition_in.introduces: The occasions that call for it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The template is a card to copy.

evidence.what: SLA CARD block: coverage, clock, target, per-stage budget, removal objectives per consumer and partner feeds, evidence.
evidence.shows: Shows removal as a row with its own objectives and the rule that nothing is sent for an ended listing.

transition_in.introduces: The record itself, field by field, to copy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark's Tradeyard SLA card of 2027 fills the card.

evidence.what: 94% of new listings covered; p95 90 seconds by end of 2028 from a 6-minute baseline; removal: search p95 10 s, every registered consumer p95 2 min, partner feeds within 15 min.
evidence.shows: Shows a target, a budget that adds up and removal objectives per consumer.

transition_in.introduces: The same template filled in once for Veldmark.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The removal row is the one the Rotterdam bike tested: removed from search a minute after the sale, it still reached 214 digests because the digest service was in no registry and re-checked nothing at send time.

evidence.what: 214 digests the next morning.
evidence.shows: Shows a consumer with no registered objective is where ended listings survive.

transition_in.introduces: The row the bike tested.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three mistakes make the card useless: a single p95 that hides the held share, budgets that do not add up, and removal objectives for the index only.

transition_in.carries_over: The card and the bike's test of it.

conclusion.heading: Using the Toolkit Over Time
conclusion.synthesis: Each template leaves evidence someone else can check only while it stays true, and the same incidents the Veldmark examples replay show how: fields for ownership, removal and dates were added after an incident found them missing, so keeping a template true means reviewing it on a calendar, adding a field when an incident finds a gap, and removing fields nobody reads.
conclusion.so_what: A team that keeps the templates as maintained data, reviewed and extended this way, finds the next missing field in a review rather than in an incident.

callback.to: The opening's claim that each template leaves evidence someone else can check, and that the fields dropped first are the ones whose absence the next incident finds.
callback.how: The reader now sees the incidents of the twelve examples as the source of those fields, and the three habits as what keeps that evidence true.

takeaway.content: Review each template on a calendar, let each post-incident review add the missing field, and remove fields filled by habit and read by nobody.

hand_off.carries_over: The toolkit's closing pointer: the glossary defines the terms the templates use.
hand_off.introduces: One definition per term, set beside the terms it is confused with, each linked to its owning chapter.

transition_in.introduces: How to keep them true over time.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each template leaves evidence someone else can check only while it stays true, above all in its fields for ownership, removal behavior and dates, and three habits keep it true: review on a calendar, let incidents add fields, and keep the set small.

evidence.what: The mass-change guard from 38,400 vanished cars, the send-time re-check from one sold bike in 214 digests, the `PublishRefused` entry from €212,000 of credits, the group-urgent change class from a rule that took three days to cross a border.
evidence.shows: Shows the fields the examples carry came from incidents, which is why a post-incident review should add one.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Fitness functions keep the records honest over a decade, the glossary defines the terms the templates use, and the bibliography lists the sources behind them.

transition_in.introduces: Where the reader goes for the terms and the sources.

decision_log.decision: Chose the twelve templates in the PLAN contract and no others: a grep of the chapters for 'toolkit' found only one explicit promise (the SLA card in publication-pipeline), already in the list.

Ordered tools by the book's parts (understand, model, supply, discover, trust, money, platform, lead) rather than by stage, so a reader can move between a tool and its chapter in reading order; the ADR is last because every other tool feeds it.

Wrote templates as tables where fields need guidance and as fenced blocks where the record is a literal artifact (share-layer row, feed contract, SLA card, policy card, consolidation card, ADR), so they can be copied as they are.
Used `bike.battery_capacity_wh` rather than the chapter's frame-size entry for Tool 4, because it shows the recommended-then-required runway; frame size appears in the common mistakes.

Spec.md success criteria not carried over as criteria: they were inventories (callouts present, twelve sections, fields trace to chapters, listed Veldmark figures, one diagram, a Sources section). The page's criteria are the three reader outcomes copied from the journal spec (find the template for a decision and a field not to drop; predict the page from its opening; reverse outline). No post-level criteria were added, to keep the criteria to what a reader can do with the page.
rejected: A custom rubric criterion that every Veldmark figure agrees with the ledger (a fact check, not a reader outcome; the ledger governs it).
A cold-reader criterion on naming one template's owner, removal and date fields (covered by AC-1's 'one field you must not leave out').

decision_log.decision: The journal entry has no thesis object, so the thesis was written here from the entry's question and R-1, and judged by a fresh thesis-rubric reader (2026-11-12: pass on all four tests). Its two notes were taken: T2 now carries 'fill only the fields that change the decision', and T3 uses the claim's causal wording. Its other note (the claim is one long sentence of three or four assertions; 'filled only where the decision changes' is its vaguest phrase) is left for the author.
